source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in RL with LLMs (ELLM)
finding: ELLM asks an LLM for goals given a text description of the agent state, then rewards the agent for doing them. This is the core idea of LLM-suggested plausibly useful behaviours.
numbers: Crafter: LLM-suggested goals 64.9% good (context-sensitive, sensible, achievable), 5% not allowed by game physics, 13.6% not context-sensitive, 16.4% not common-sense. Uses Codex; Housekeep uses text-davinci-002.
quote: Rewards agent for achieving goals suggested by a language model prompted with a description of the agent's current state.
limits: Goal quality is only about two thirds good. Needs a captioner that turns states into text.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S3 priors: ask the model for plausible next goals from the current state, then filter. Expect about a third to be junk.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in RL with LLMs (ELLM) - exploration results
finding: In Crafter, ELLM unlocks more achievements than novelty-only methods, but fewer than a hard-coded oracle.
numbers: About 6 unique achievements per episode for ELLM vs 9 for the ground-truth Oracle; RND, APT and Novelty baselines stay under 3. Goal-conditioning gave no significant advantage.
limits: Pretraining achievements only. Downstream fine-tuning on Crafter was unreliable for ALL methods (agent unlearned skills when reward scale changed).
agent_relevance: LLM priors roughly double coverage of useful behaviour versus pure novelty, yet leave a gap to a perfect prior. Keep the novelty bias (reward each goal once) as a guard.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in RL with LLMs (ELLM) - Housekeep and model size
finding: In Housekeep, LLM accuracy on which object belongs where limits the exploration gain. Smaller GPT-3 models were worse.
numbers: LLM caught mismatches (e.g. vase in kitchen sink) with accuracy above 87%, but accuracy on correct matches ranged 50-90% by scene. ELLM had higher pretraining success in 3 of 4 tasks. Initial smaller GPT-3 models gave degraded performance, so Codex/Davinci were used.
limits: Only 4 single-room scenes, 5 misplaced objects each. Caching was essential: uncached, a 5M-step run would spend about 27 hours on API calls.
agent_relevance: Prior quality drives results; false negatives hurt most when few answers are correct. Cache and reuse model suggestions.

source: Klissarov et al. (2023) Motif: Intrinsic Motivation from AI Feedback
finding: Motif has Llama 2 70B rank pairs of NetHack event messages, trains a reward model on those rankings, and uses it as intrinsic reward. The agent gets a higher game score from this reward alone than from the real score reward.
numbers: NetHack score task: Motif intrinsic reward only beats baselines that optimise score directly. Sparse staircase level 3 and 4 tasks: extrinsic-only and RND success = 0, Motif above 0. Oracle task: about 30% success with intrinsic plus extrinsic reward, where no method had made progress without demonstrations.
quote: Surprisingly, by only learning to maximize its intrinsic reward, Motif achieves a higher game score than an algorithm directly trained to maximize the score itself.
limits: Needs text messages in the game; about 10-20% of screens have one. Response parse rate about 90%.
agent_relevance: Evidence that LLM judgement of progress (not goal generation) is a usable prior. Preferences between pairs are easier for a model than absolute scores.

source: Klissarov et al. (2023) Motif: Intrinsic Motivation from AI Feedback - scale and prompt
finding: Bigger annotator models give better agents; a one-sentence hint helps; tiny prompt rewording changes behaviour.
numbers: Success on staircase level 3 rises from Llama 2 7B to 13B to 70B. Zero-knowledge prompt still works; adding one sentence of task hint significantly boosts score. A reworded, semantically similar prompt: default-prompt agent found a reward hack, reworded-prompt agent went down the dungeon.
limits: Scaling shown on one task. Score task showed no significant difference between prompt wordings, but the oracle task did.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording changes which prior is distilled, so wording is a hidden variable. Test two or more phrasings of any prior prompt.

source: Klissarov et al. (2023) Motif: Intrinsic Motivation from AI Feedback - reward hacking
finding: On the oracle task the combined reward was gamed: the agent killed a yellow mold, ate its corpse and hallucinated, which made the oracle appear. Alignment broke when combined with environment reward.
numbers: Oracle success about 30% overall, but with the default prompt the hallucination trick replaced intended descent.
limits: Single environment; mechanism shown in the paper's Figure 5.
agent_relevance: LLM priors can be exploited once a search process optimises against them. Guard S3 priors against being used as the target.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) OMNI: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness
finding: An LLM judges which learnable tasks are interesting. Combined with learning progress, it beats learning progress alone and uniform sampling.
numbers: Crafter (10 seeds, 100M steps): uniform learns 4 tasks, 3 interesting; learning progress 55 tasks, 9 interesting; OMNI 82 tasks, 14 interesting. Mean success on interesting tasks: 0.103 uniform, 0.52 LP, 0.78 OMNI. BabyAI tasks learned: 1, 4 and 8.
limits: OMNI vs LP p<1e-3 (Mann-Whitney). Boring tasks were synthetic (repeated, compound, synonym).
agent_relevance: Use the model as a filter over candidate directions, on top of a measure of learnability or progress, not instead of it.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) OMNI: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness - oracle comparison
finding: The model-based interestingness filter is almost as good as a hand-built oracle.
numbers: Across metrics, differences between OMNI and LP+oracle at 25/50/75/100% of training are not significant (all but one p>0.05).
limits: Oracle was hand designed by the authors for these tasks; the FM prompt had few-shot examples. Authors note Goodhart risk when the filter becomes an optimisation target.
agent_relevance: The filter does not need to be perfect to match a human-built prior. Watch for Goodhart effects.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can LLMs Explore In-Context?
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs fail to explore reliably in multi-armed bandits unless the prompt is heavily engineered.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2-13B; 5 arms gap 0.2 (hard), 4 arms gap 0.5 (easy); 48 configs each for GPT-3.5 and Llama2, 72 for GPT-4. Only 1 config (GPT-4, suggestive hint, summarised history as per-arm averages, zero-shot CoT) explores well. Basic GPT-4 prompt: suffix failure in >60% of replicates (T=500, N=20).
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Bandits are simpler than real tasks; authors say external summarisation may be impossible in complex settings. NeurIPS 2024.
agent_relevance: LLMs do not self-explore. The explore step must be built into the scaffold with summarised history and an explicit hint.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can LLMs Explore In-Context? - failure modes
finding: Two failure types: suffix failure (best arm never picked after early rounds) and uniform-like failure (arms picked almost equally).
numbers: Only 3 GPT-4 configurations avoid suffix failures in the T=100 runs; 2 of those show uniform-like failure and 1 (BSSC0) succeeds. GPT-3.5 and Llama2 were worse in all experiments. The same config without summarisation fails.
limits: T=100 main runs, N=10 or 20 replicates.
agent_relevance: Check for premature lock-in and for aimless spread; both are measurable from the arm-choice history.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 on Wilson's horizon task (two-armed bandit): good regret, but little sign of directed exploration.
numbers: Regret: GPT-3 M=2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans 3.24 (SD 10.26), t(38878)=-5.03, p<.001. Short horizon: GPT-3 equals humans (p=.97). Long-horizon start: GPT-3 lower regret than humans (p<.001). Random-exploration effect of reward difference beta=0.18, z=14.48.
quote: GPT-3 had a tendency to repeat previously observed options.
limits: GPT-3; human data from a prior study. Paper reports rudimentary random exploration; the strategic long-horizon increase seen in people was not found in the passage read.
agent_relevance: Models act like exploiters with noise and repeat previously seen options. Do not expect an uncertainty bonus from the model unprompted.

source: Nie et al. (2024) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration
finding: BanditBench shows LLMs lag classic bandit algorithms, but giving UCB-style support in the prompt or distilling UCB data improves them, even for smaller models.
numbers: Gemini-1.5 Flash and Pro, Gemma-2B etc; 16 MAB configs and 2 contextual configs, win-rate metric. Few-shot demos of UCB: summarised history 50.2% win-rate vs raw history 27.5%. Fine-tuning on UCB: raw history 65.6% vs summarised 28.3%. Fine-tuned Flash approaches UCB on contextual bandits.
limits: Win-rate is relative to the pool of models tested. Table layouts garbled in text extraction, so only values stated in the text are used.
agent_relevance: Give the model the explore-bonus numbers (algorithm-guided support). Summaries help prompting; raw logs help training.

source: Nie et al. (2024) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration - demo difficulty
finding: Which demonstrations help depends on the method: few-shot likes easy demos, fine-tuning likes hard ones.
numbers: Few-shot: 50.2 win-rate with easy demos vs 43.0 with hard. Fine-tuning: 65.6 with hard vs 54.5 with easy.
limits: Study is bandits only.
agent_relevance: S3 prior: pair LLM suggestions with an explicit count-based uncertainty score computed outside the model; keep in-context examples simple.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with LLMs
finding: Voyager uses GPT-4 as an automatic curriculum that proposes the next task from agent state, a skill library of verified code, and self-verification. A full LLM-agent loop of language-guided exploration.
numbers: Minecraft: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x more than baselines; 2.3x longer distances. Tech tree (3 runs): iron tool in 21 +/-7 iterations (3/3) vs AutoGPT 135 +/-103 (3/3); ReAct and Reflexion 0/3. Diamond tool only 1/3 for Voyager.
limits: Only 3 trials per tech-tree cell. Uses GPT-4 code generation; text only.
agent_relevance: Curriculum from state plus verified skill memory is a working loop for S3 to operators.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with LLMs - ablations
finding: Removing the automatic curriculum or self-verification collapses exploration.
numbers: Random curriculum: discovered items drop 93%. No self-verification: -73%. GPT-4 gets 5.7x more unique items than GPT-3.5 for code. Zero-shot unseen tasks (50 iterations): Voyager 3/3 on diamond pickaxe in 19 +/-3 iterations; ReAct, Reflexion, AutoGPT 0/3.
limits: A hand-made curriculum was also worse than the automatic one, numbers only in a figure.
agent_relevance: Self-verification is the most valuable guard. Context-aware task proposal beats a fixed order.

source: Bougie and Watanabe (2024) Exploring Beyond Curiosity Rewards: Language-Driven Exploration in RL (iLLM)
finding: iLLM uses an LLM for two tasks: action generation and history compression. State-action pairs map into LLM token embeddings via a Hopfield module, so no text description is required.
numbers: Crafter: about 7 unique achievements per episode vs 6 for best baseline. BabyAI PickUpLoc: RND and NGU still under 0.25 after 100M steps, iLLM(hop) reaches 0.85 after 68M steps. Nine BabyAI-Text tasks, 10 seeds.
limits: Table cell numbers lost in text extraction; only numbers stated in prose used. ELLM capped by LLM mistakes in MiniHack.
agent_relevance: Compressing history with the model is itself an exploration signal; matches the S3 idea of a fast prior over what is worth trying.

source: Bougie and Watanabe (2024) Exploring Beyond Curiosity Rewards: Language-Driven Exploration in RL (iLLM) - robustness and backbone
finding: iLLM resists noisy-TV style traps and gets slightly better with bigger LLM backbones.
numbers: Average return over 9 BabyAI-Text tasks: Transformer-XL 280M 0.83-0.85, Flan-T5 780M 0.75-0.79, Llama-2 7B 0.87-0.88 (two input variants each). Under noise, iLLM scores significantly higher than baselines (paired t-test, p<0.002).
limits: On Atari, RND/NGU scored near zero; iLLM beat non-LLM baselines on 4 named games. Where the LLM has less domain knowledge, gains were smaller.
agent_relevance: Language priors help most where the model has domain knowledge; gains shrink elsewhere.

source: Lu, Hu and Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore
finding: IGE replaces Go-Explore's hand-made heuristics with a foundation model that picks which archived state to return to, which action to try, and whether a new state is interesting. It is an LLM agent loop with an archive.
numbers: Game of 24: 100% success 70.8% faster than best baseline (DFS), significant at 150 operations (chi-sq p<0.05); Tree of Thoughts reported 74%. TextWorld Cooking: beats ReAct by 36 points; Coin Collector: only IGE solves it, all others fail. Reflexion did not improve over ReAct and often lowered scores in long horizons.
limits: GPT-4o main model; also checked with Claude Sonnet 3.5 and an open model. Archive filtering controls context length.
agent_relevance: Keep an archive of promising states and let the model prune it. Pruning prevents context bloat.

source: Lu, Hu and Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore - ablations and domain-general prompts
finding: Model-based state selection and archive filtering matter most in long-horizon tasks. Minimal prompts keep most of the advantage.
numbers: Paper reports IGE keeps a significant advantage with domain-general prompts (Table 5) and that filtering sharply shrinks the archive (Table 4).
limits: Exact figures sit in tables not captured by text extraction.
agent_relevance: Prior prompts need not be task-tuned to help.

source: Faldor et al. (2025) OMNI-EPIC
finding: Extends OMNI: the model writes code for new environments and reward functions, and judges them for interestingness and learnability against an archive.
numbers: Short runs with RL, 5 repeats: OMNI-EPIC significantly beats controls on ANNECS and ANNECS-OMNI. A 50-participant human study checked the automated success detector.
limits: Compute heavy; the success detector is itself model-based.
agent_relevance: The model can propose both goals and the checks that decide success; checks need human audit.

source: Paglieri et al. (2024) BALROG: Benchmarking agentic LLM and VLM reasoning on games
finding: Zero-shot LLM agents show weak systematic exploration across game suites.
numbers: Best language-only average progress 32.64% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet); GPT-4o and Llama 3.1 70B a few points behind. NetHack: best model o1-preview 1.5% progression. No model solved MiniHack quest or boxoban. In Coin Collector agents wander and revisit rooms.
limits: Zero-shot, no exploration scaffold.
agent_relevance: Without a scaffold the model does not explore; knowing a good action does not mean it acts on it.

source: Paglieri et al. (2024) BALROG: Benchmarking agentic LLM and VLM reasoning on games - knowing-doing gap
finding: Models take actions they know are bad, for example leaving the dungeon early in NetHack.
numbers: Qualitative, across NetHack runs. Llama models led Baba Is AI language-only by a 10% margin over GPT-4o.
quote: models often exit the dungeon shortly after starting the game
limits: Agent prompts are zero-shot.
agent_relevance: S3 priors must be tied to action checks; knowledge in the prompt is not enough.

source: Cross-paper synthesis (ELLM, iLLM, Motif, OMNI, IGE, EVOLvE, Krishnamurthy)
finding: Pattern across studies: models are good at proposing or ranking what is plausibly useful, and poor at managing exploration themselves.
numbers: ELLM 64.9% good goals; Motif beats the score reward; OMNI 14 vs 9 interesting tasks; unscaffolded bandits: only 1 working GPT-4 configuration (Krishnamurthy).
limits: Different environments, no shared benchmark; most are RL-training studies, not pure prompting.
agent_relevance: Use the model for generation and ranking (S3); use code-side counts and archives for the exploration control.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in RL with LLMs (ELLM) - finetuning failure
finding: Fine-tuning an ELLM-pretrained policy on Crafter downstream tasks was unreliable for all methods; guided exploration use of the frozen policy worked better.
numbers: Agent unlearned earlier skills early in fine-tuning; lower learning rate, frozen layers and reward rescaling only partly helped and cost sample efficiency.
limits: Crafter only; Housekeep showed only minor dips because pretraining and finetuning tasks were similar.
agent_relevance: A prior should shape what is tried, not overwrite what is learned. Mismatch between prior goals and the real task reward causes loss of useful behaviour.

source: Lu, Hu and Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore - Reflexion in long horizons
finding: Reflexion did not help in long-horizon exploration because history grew too long; archive filtering kept context short.
numbers: Reflexion did not improve over ReAct in any tested game and tended to lower performance (authors' hypothesis: long history).
limits: Hypothesis, not tested by direct ablation.
agent_relevance: Reflection over whole histories can hurt; selection of interesting states is a better memory.
